# external-cluster

A cluster something else brings into existence, which this lab installs into.

<!-- Generated by nix build .#referencePages -->

## Inputs

| input | type | default | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| assignsLoadBalancers | boolean | `true` | Whether a `LoadBalancer` Service gets an address here.  True by default because every managed Kubernetes offering has a cloud controller that assigns one — which is the case this floe mostly covers, and the opposite of the bare Talos default.  |
| context | string | *(required)* |        kubectl context this cluster answers on.         A decision, not a discovery: `cata` writes the kubeconfig under this        name after fetching it, rather than taking whatever the producing tool        called it. That is what keeps `KUBERNETES_CLUSTER.context` concrete even though the cluster's endpoint is not.  |
| distribution | string | `"kubernetes"` | What it runs, for the record and for drift reporting. |
| edgeMode | one of "self", "none" | `"self"` | Who fronts it.  Never `proxy`: the lab's proxy reaches backends on its own docker network, and a cluster this lab did not create is not on it. `self` says the cluster is its own edge, which is what a managed cluster with a LoadBalancer is.  |
| kubeconfigKey | null or string | `null` | Key this cluster's kubeconfig is published under, when a state-based apply is what produced it. *Which* store is resolved — `optional.labStore`.  Null for a cluster a controller in another cluster reconciles: there the kubeconfig is in a connection Secret and the lab reaches it through the management cluster's `provisions` declaration instead. One of the two has to say how the cluster becomes reachable, and a lab check refuses one that says neither — a cluster the lab deploys to and has no kubeconfig for fails at the first kubectl call with a context that does not exist.  |
| madeBy | string | `""` | What brings it into existence, for the operator reading a plan.  Free text and never dispatched on, for a cluster nothing in this lab creates. One that *is* created by something here says so through `optional.provisioning` instead, where the planner can read it — and a cluster that answers neither is refused, because a cluster nothing creates and nothing fetches a kubeconfig for is a context that will not exist.  A `create-cluster` step that does nothing reads as broken; one that says what it is waiting for reads as waiting.  |
| name | string | *(required)* | Cluster name, as members and the kubeconfig see it. Required. |
| podSubnet | string | *(required)* | Pod CIDR.  Required rather than defaulted, because for a cluster this lab does not create, a default would be a guess about somebody else's network that every member then renders against. Declared here and checked against the cluster it turns out to be.  |
| serviceSubnet | string | *(required)* | Service CIDR. Same reasoning as `podSubnet`. |
| version | string | `"1.31"` | Kubernetes minor version this cluster answers as. |
| wait | string | `"10m"` | How long to wait for the API server to answer once the cluster has been created.  Here rather than on the cluster, because how long a cluster takes to come up is a property of what makes it. The wait for an *apply* to settle belongs to whatever applies, and is `DELIVERY_POLICY`'s.  |

## What it emits

Rendered by `provisions` as the lab unit `workload-provisioner`. A unit of the lab
installs nothing into a cluster, and its provisions are sealed inside the
lab's inclusion — so its declaration above is its interface.
